Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2+4\textrm{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PCP^{-1}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/4a53548a17d9b4fd870ce70285bfc2c57cf6c8d352f75149e5aa7511ef4af853.png)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

First, notice that 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/aa5738b600440bf8327670fc21cd8005c660def232119b2b4808237d988367bd.png)

while

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/fc91fcabd47720075061e670f62be9ea9b636070a05cba70752bb7060608b764.png)

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overline{\lambda}=2-4\textrm{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda.$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overline{\mathbf{v}},$ the complex conjugate of $\mathbf{v}.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 7\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3+4\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
